title: What happens at Communion?
intro: Jesus took bread and wine at the Last Supper and said, “This is My body… this is My blood.” Almost all Christians share this meal (called the Eucharist, Mass, Divine Liturgy, Holy Communion or the Lord’s Supper), but they understand Jesus’ words in different ways.

views.label: The bread and wine become Christ’s body and blood
views.summary: Catholics teach transubstantiation: the substance of the bread and wine becomes Christ’s body and blood while their appearance remains. The Orthodox and other ancient Eastern churches also teach a real change, but prefer not to define how. The Eucharist also makes present Christ’s one sacrifice.
views.source: Catechism of the Catholic Church 1374–1376; Confession of Dositheus, Decree 17

views.label: Christ is truly present in, with and under the bread and wine
views.summary: Lutherans teach that Christ’s true body and blood are present together with the bread and wine, which remain bread and wine, and are received by all who eat and drink.
views.source: Augsburg Confession, Article X; Luther’s Small Catechism

views.label: Christ is present spiritually, received by faith
views.summary: In the Reformed view, held also by many Anglicans and Methodists, believers truly feed on Christ by faith through the Holy Spirit, but the bread and wine are not changed.
views.source: Westminster Confession 29.7; Thirty-Nine Articles, Article XXVIII

views.label: A memorial and proclamation of Christ’s death
views.summary: Many Baptists, Pentecostals, Anabaptists and others see the Supper as a symbolic act of remembrance and obedience, proclaiming Christ’s death until he comes.
views.source: Baptist Faith and Message (2000), Article VII

common: All these traditions agree that Jesus commanded this meal, that it remembers his death, and that it is deeply important. Quakers observe no outward Communion, seeking inward communion with Christ.
